item.title: Before You Mock the "Helicopter Mom"
item.description:
Parenting

Before You Mock the "Helicopter Mom"

Contextualizing, de-stigmatizing, and effectively supporting moms who "hover."

Posted September 2, 2026

Key points
  • Girls are socialized to manage others' distress, making maternal over-involvement practically inevitable.
  • Over-parenting can impair children's distress tolerance and capacity for independence.
  • Telling burnt-out moms to "do less" without addressing systemic causes increases shame, not change.
  • Healing begins with context, not directives — self-compassion and curiosity outperform guilt every time.

Society is not at a loss for eye-rolls when it comes to "helicopter moms" (HMs). The term falls under the "over-parenting" umbrella and describes mothers who "hover" (too) closely above their children to surveil for potential "danger" — physical or emotional — and often intervene in the name of "protection."

Critics cite research showing that developmentally inappropriate parental micro-management can stunt a child's eventual capacity to function as an autonomous adult, as well as data indicating this parenting style can negatively impact a mother's mental health in ways that put children's mental health at risk, too. Some more simply wonder: "Can't these women find anything better to do with their time?"

Source: Millerium Arkay / Shutterstock

The context surrounding HMs, though — the sociological, psychological, and biological factors that explain why they started helicoptering in the first place — is conspicuously absent from these conversations.

To consider this context is to humanize these women — a crucial prerequisite to offering them support; or maybe, even, a parachute back down to earth.

How'd She Get All The Way Up There, Anyway?

Find me a mother who actively sets an intention to helicopter her children. I'll wait.

A more likely story? Her ascension to high-altitude parenting was slow and steady over a lifetime of powerful messaging that made "hovering" practically inevitable.

Young girls are generally socialized to be emotionally attuned — and relationally responsive — to others' emotional discomfort. The message: "good girls" know that other people's emotions are, to an extent, their responsibility to both anticipate and manage (Chaplin & Aldao, 2013).

Source: Irina WS / Shutterstock

When girls become women and women become mothers, there is a gradual shift in messaging from what "good girls" do to what "good mothers" do.

The dominating cultural belief system that dictates how society thinks about "good mothering" — and has for centuries — is called "Intensive Mothering Ideology" (IMI). It posits that "good mothers" neglect their own needs to focus on "optimizing" their child's development (Hays, 1996). Despite research denouncing it as a "gold standard" approach to mothering, its grip has only tightened with the rise of social media in recent years (Şenöz & Karaduman, 2026).

There is also a biological reality to consider: a mother's nervous system is primed to respond to her child's pain as if it were her own (Riem et al., 2012). Moms who avoid pain on behalf of their children are also, whether they realize it or not, sparing themselves — a powerful reinforcer indeed. Neurodivergent mothers are particularly susceptible to this physiological vulnerability.

Source: Roman Samborskyi / Shutterstock

Another consideration is our culture's tendency to reward a "more is more" approach to any valued role or task. It's why the employee who takes on the extra projects is the same one who gets the promotion. "Hard work pays off."

Surely, then, this same logic must apply to the role of "mother," regarded near-universally not just as a "valued" role but as a role that is no less than sacred?

Well...sort of.

The job description for "mom" is verbose. Some aspects of the gig, like "loving," fit easily into the "more is more" mold: a mother's love knows no bounds, and is best served unconditionally.

Effective "parenting," however, is not (always) synonymous with expending maximum effort; it requires discernment: to step in or to step back; to shield from pain or to allow for it; to solve or to wait?

Instead of explaining why this confusion is a product of lifelong conditioning, though, we shame them. We wonder, awestruck, "how could they not have known that 'more is more' until it's not?"

Importantly, the degree to which over-parenting can be more "harmful" than "helpful" is different for every family. Children with special needs and/or certain vulnerabilities may genuinely require levels of advocacy that look like helicoptering from the outside but are, in fact, appropriate and necessary.

Why "Do Less" Doesn't Quite Land

Source: Pathdoc / Shutterstock

Maybe HMs do need to "do less," and this "tip" is an astonishingly inadequate instruction for a woman whose entire developmental history taught her that other people's distress is hers to fix.

I do not dispute that over-parenting has a negative impact on kids.

What I do dispute — nay, resent — is how some "experts" respond to HMs seeking support: with parenting directives that fail to consider their positions in context (e.g., "do less"). These "pointers" are likely to produce shame far faster than they will inspire behavior change.

It would be more effective to first educate moms on how their style of over-parenting came to be, and only in a voice that is nonjudgmental and contextually-informed. Meaningful behavior change cannot occur while shame is still in the room.

Only then might HMs be able to process that hovering might feel "safe," and that we often best support our children by walking alongside them.

A Misnomer

"Helicoptering" has become shorthand for, "a mother with a personal problem" — a nagging, irrational need to do too much for her kids, to the point of damaging their development. Why can't she just trust her child? Tolerate some discomfort? Get a life?

Another phenomenon that disproportionately affects high-achieving women, imposter syndrome, used to be similarly framed as a "personal flaw." More recently, though, it has been reframed as a systemic issue — a predictable response to environments steeped in bias, exclusion, and relentless scrutiny — being used to pathologize the people those systems are failing.

Don't moms who over-parent deserve a similar, personally blameless reframe?

A Soft Landing

It is not necessarily a mother's fault when she engages in helicoptering behaviors, and she is the only one who can change the way she parents.

Supporting her on her healing journey comes in many forms, including:

Source: Look Studio / Shutterstock

  • rejecting gendered messaging that encourages girls to prioritize others' emotions over their own

  • rejecting pro-IMI social media communities built around "more is more"-fueled performances rather than shared values

  • naming the utter absence of institutional support for mothers and fighting for better support

  • holding patriarchal systems that may use their power to maintain a status quo that benefits them accountable

  • training providers to begin treatment by exonerating HMs from shame (instead of leading with "simple" parenting tips)

Let's quit the eye rolls and commit to really seeing these women for who they are: well-meaning mothers who care deeply for their children (and are owed a great deal more than a label).

item.title: When Secrets Put Teen Lives at Risk
item.description:
Adolescence

When Secrets Put Teen Lives at Risk

How to talk to your kid about breaking a friend’s trust to save their life.

Posted September 2, 2026

Key points
  • Teens overwhelmingly see telling an adult about a friend's self-harm as betrayal, not help.
  • Teens disclose based on who feels safe, not who's actually equipped to help.
  • A friendship can be rebuilt or replaced. A person cannot.

Last weekend, I led a two-hour workshop for 50 teens about mental health stigma and how to get better at asking for and offering help. I created one activity: help or harm. I read a statement aloud, and the teens yelled out “help” if they thought the action was helpful, or “harm” if it was harmful.

This was the last statement I read: “Texting a friend’s parent behind their back because you are worried about them.” And the room erupted in a mess of “help” and “harm” shouted over each other. When I asked for a show of hands for who thought this was harmful, an overwhelming number of hands shot up.

“Does your answer change if you are scared your friend is going to hurt themselves?” I asked.

A few hands went down, but not many.

I asked why they thought it was harmful.

“Because then your friend won’t trust you.”

“Because no one wants someone going behind their back.”

“Because you’re gonna get them in trouble with their parents.”

Every one of those reasons made complete sense to me. That’s exactly why this is one of the most important conversations a parent can have with their kid.

What I Decided in 8th Grade

When I was in 8th grade, I saw one of my friends cutting herself. She had scars up and down her legs and arms, although she tried to hide them under long sleeves and pants. When she noticed me looking at her scars, she asked me to promise not to tell anyone.

I promised.

That night, I felt sick. I knew that she needed help, even though she said she didn’t. But I’d made a promise, and I kept my promises.

Lying in bed, I asked myself, “What’s the worst thing that could happen if I don’t say anything?” She could die. And I’d spend the rest of my life knowing I had information that might have prevented this, but I was silent because I didn’t want to break a promise.

I decided on something that has stuck with me for over a decade: I’d rather lose my friendship than lose my friend. Betraying my friend felt awful, but it was a risk I could and did recover from. You can rebuild a friendship or make more friends. You cannot bring someone back once they are gone.

Why Parents Need to Have This Conversation

This isn’t a decision kids make on their own, and it's evident in the answers I get every time I run this activity. Kids have learned over the years that betraying a friend’s trust is wrong, and that promises are meant to be kept.

These instincts aren’t wrong. They are useful in many situations. But when safety is on the line, this reasoning is incomplete.

Research backs up what I saw in the room last weekend. A study published in the Journal of Abnormal Child Psychology found that when adolescents disclose suicidal or self-harm behaviors to a friend, only 12 percent of those friends suggest telling an adult. The rest kept it between them, which aligns with what researchers keep finding: teens disclose based on who feels safe, not who is in the best position to help.

According to the World Health Organization, suicide is the third leading cause of death among people aged 15 to 29 worldwide. This isn’t rare. It’s the kind of situation most teens will face at least once, whether it's them or a peer.

I’ve had to tell an adult about a friend or classmate who was hurting themselves on numerous occasions, and it never got easier. Each time felt just as gut-wrenching as the first. But years later, each one of those people is still alive. And that’s truly the only outcome I care about.

What Your Kid Needs to Hear From You

Tell them directly that if a friend is struggling with their mental health or talking about wanting to hurt themselves, telling an adult is not betrayal. It’s actually the most loyal thing you can do, even if it doesn’t feel that way in the moment.

Tell them that you will never be angry at them for coming to you or another adult with a friend’s secret.

Give your kid actual words they can use with their friends.

“I’m worried about you, and I need to tell someone.”

“I care about you too much to keep this to myself.”

“I’m not doing this to get you in trouble. I’m doing it because I don’t want to lose you.”

Tell them that the friendship might get messy after. The friend might be upset. Things may be awkward. That discomfort is real and difficult to deal with, but it’s survivable. Losing a friend is not.

Tell them that if they ever think about harming themselves, they can come to you no matter what. And tell them that if they don’t want to go to you, they need to go to another adult to get support. Let them know that you care more about them getting the help they need than being the one to give it.

This conversation might feel awkward to have early on, but it will be unbearable to have once it’s too late.

item.title: What Your Regrets Can Teach You
item.description:
Guilt

What Your Regrets Can Teach You

Embedded in your regrets are lessons to be learned.

Posted September 2, 2026

Key points
  • We all can look back at our lives and find things that we regret—either isolated events or patterns.
  • Common regrets are not pushing forward or not holding back, not being brave or not being restrained.
  • The patterns are clues to lessons to learn. Find and apply the lessons and you'll run your life better.
Source: tumisu/pixabay

We all have regrets. You look back on your life and can still feel the sting of that hurtful remark you made to your high school girlfriend, or you replay, unexpectedly at 3 a.m. while lying in bed, that time you had too much to drink at a friend’s party and acted like a jerk. These are isolated, yet regrettable events.

Patterns

But then there are regrets that are not one-time events but, instead, are part and parcel of a larger pattern. These are patterns that signal when our lives are going off course from our character, needs, and values. Here are some of the common patterns of regret that I’ve heard from clients over the years:

  • Not listening to their gut or trusting their instincts
  • Not being brave enough to take the harder, riskier path
  • Quitting too soon—a job, a relationship—or not trying harder
  • Holding grudges or not forgiving others
  • Continuing to treat someone badly, taking them for granted, and not showing more appreciation
  • Not being more open and letting others in

Looking at this list, we can see some themes. Regrets may have to do with not pushing forward (listening to one's gut, being brave, taking risks), with not holding back (resentments, quitting), or not being more generous (offering forgiveness, appreciation, openness). Overall, these are themes that tell us how to shift direction and change how we run our lives.

What are your lessons?

Here are several questions to help you uncover the lessons beneath your regrets:

  1. Think back over your life; either see it as a movie moving forward, or begin with those familiar instances that have continued to linger. Are they isolated events, a result of your youth and inexperience, or something larger and part of a pattern that perhaps continues to this day?
  2. When you gather all these memories together, is there a core theme, a moral to this part of the story of your life so far? What was missing most from your life’s equation? What do you wish you had done that you didn’t?
  3. Do you have a theory about why you behave this way?
  4. Again, looking back, has this pattern changed? Have you become better at learning the lessons and skills you were challenged to develop—for example, have you become more open, more generous, more forgiving, or braver?
  5. What is the take-away? What is it you need to focus on and work on changing the most to eliminate your regrets and be more proud of yourself?

Life is a process that involves realizing you’ve made mistakes, learning from them, and moving on instead of dwelling on them and beating yourself up. It's a process of realizing that even the negative holds something positive and believing that your life is working for you, helping you become the person you need to be.

item.title: When Did Avoidant Attachment Become the Villain?
item.description:
Attachment

When Did Avoidant Attachment Become the Villain?

How attachment theory became a tool for blame instead of understanding.

Posted September 2, 2026

Key points
  • Avoidant attachment is about how someone responds to relational distress, not a fear of commitment.
  • Insecure attachment style can help us understand conflict patterns without assigning judgment or blame.
  • Compassion can help people navigate close relationships, which can be challenging.

As more people have learned about attachment theory, it’s shifted from a research-based framework for understanding conflict patterns to a way we oversimplify and judge others. Nowhere is this clearer than with avoidant attachment, which has become shorthand for commitment phobia, conflict avoidance, unjustified breakups, and a lack of empathy. Just type “avoidant” into social media, and you’ll get endless posts and videos of how someone with this attachment style was wrong and how to make sure you don’t fall into a relationship with them.

Why do we feel the need to vilify people with an insecure attachment? Relationships are hard, and we should give people more grace as they navigate them. This requires a more compassionate understanding of avoidant attachment and how it’s currently being misunderstood.

The Negative Perception of Avoidant Attachment Style

Attachment theory suggests that people develop different patterns for seeking closeness and responding to perceived threats to important relationships (like arguments). Early relationships with caregivers help shape attachment patterns that can carry into our adult relationships. When a relationship feels threatened, some people desperately seek to reestablish closeness (anxious attachment style), others pull away to manage the hurt (avoidant attachment style), and others do a confusing mix of both (disorganized attachment style).

Some (perhaps many?) believe that people with an avoidant attachment lure you into a close connection and then disappear the second it gets serious or faces adversity. However, the belief that people with this attachment style cannot commit to romantic relationships is just plain wrong.

People with avoidant attachment are more likely to pull away during conflict. They often feel inadequate or overwhelmed and fear conflict will escalate or threaten the relationship, and then they distance themselves.

Unfortunately, withdrawing often has the opposite intended effect. Instead of creating calm, it can make the other person feel unheard or dismissed, often leading to bigger feelings and an even more urgent desire to talk.

People with avoidant attachment can contribute to making conflicts worse and, yes, to relationships breaking down or ending. But people with anxious attachment can, too, as their intense pursuit of resolution and reconnection can escalate arguments by not allowing their partner space to regulate or think.

What We Get Wrong About Avoidant Attachment

An avoidant attachment style is not the same as avoiding commitment. The attachment style is more about how people respond to relationship tension or conflict than whether they can deepen or invest in a romantic partnership.

It feels easy to say that our relationship ended because our partner with an avoidant attachment couldn’t handle being close to us. It feels better than developing a more nuanced understanding, which likely includes perfectly reasonable motives for the person ending things and perhaps ways in which we contributed to the relationship’s demise, too. We are in distress and emotionally raw when someone has left us, and we want an explanation for how they could hurt us like that. Claiming that the person is avoidant means that they left because of them and their emotional deficiencies, not because we did something wrong or were insufficient.

Although it’s an easy explanation to grab, an avoidant attachment style isn’t always the reason someone leaves a relationship. It could be for legitimate reasons and have nothing to do with attachment patterns. Perhaps the other person became aggressive when angry, was dismissive or rude, or wanted different things out of life.

Or maybe we can agree that sometimes no one is to blame because not every romantic relationship is meant to last, and that’s okay. We have to allow relationships to end without making someone a villain.

Attachment Styles Aren't Character Flaws

People with an avoidant attachment style don't necessarily withdraw from conflict because they don't care. Often, they withdraw because the conflict feels overwhelming or threatening and they truly don't know what else to do. They’re afraid that talking will make the fight worse and hope the problems might go away if they’re no longer the focus.

It may appear as though they are cold or withholding, and can certainly feel that way, but their withdrawal is a reaction to overwhelm, not evidence of heartlessness. Someone with an avoidant attachment style may have learned that directly addressing problems is unsafe, ineffective, or likely to make things worse.

You can hold them accountable for avoiding hard conversations while also remembering that this behavior is protective, not punitive. Their goal usually isn’t to hurt you; it’s to stabilize what feels like a rocky situation in your relationship.

Perhaps the best way to develop empathy aside from a deeper understanding of this attachment style is to remember that all of us, even if you have a secure attachment, engage in unhelpful behaviors at times. Whether it’s lashing out, running away, being defensive, minimizing the issue, or making relational threats, we can all behave poorly when we are in distress. We want the problem to go away, and we’re trying desperately to make that happen, even if the strategies we’re using are having the opposite effect.

Most people aren’t intentionally trying to damage their meaningful relationships. Instead, they are using the only strategies they know to try to fix things. And while these strategies may not work, or may even do further harm, we can still view them with deeper nuance instead of assuming malicious intent.

Somewhere along the way, attachment styles stopped being an explanation for how people handle relational distress and became a way to judge them. Secure is good, anxious is needy, avoidant is cruel. The moralization of attachment theory has allowed for unfair generalizations, character judgments, and shame. Attachment styles can help us understand behavior, but they shouldn't determine how we judge the person behind it. Understanding isn't an excuse for bad behavior; it's an explanation that allows for accountability with more compassion.

item.title: Crying as a Way of Knowing
item.description:
Emotions

Crying as a Way of Knowing

What our tears are trying to tell us.

Posted September 2, 2026

Key points
  • Emotional tears appear to be uniquely human.
  • Crying can help us process our emotions and leave us calmer, clearer, and more reconciled to life.
  • Our tears can reveal what matters to us before we consciously know it ourselves.
Source: Pixabay/pixelwanderer/public domain

In many cultures, especially for men, crying is considered to be undignified and infantile behavior, except in certain specific circumstances, such as mourning the loss of a relative. After childhood, men shed tears much less frequently than women. The reasons for this are partly biological, but mainly sociocultural.

“Crying,” or “tearing up,” is not just one thing. There are in fact three types of tears, two of which are rather uninteresting: basal tears that lubricate and protect the eye, and reflex tears that flush out irritants such as smoke particles or onion vapors. The third type of tear is, of course, shed in response to emotion.

Crocodile Tears

Whereas many animals have basal and reflex tears, emotional tears appear to be uniquely human. Although other animals, of course, vocalize and express distress, there is no convincing evidence that they shed tears for emotional reasons. So, presumably, if women cry more often than men, it is because they are more human? Elephants and chimpanzees are sometimes said to “weep,” but it has not been conclusively demonstrated that these are indeed emotional tears. On the other hand, we can be pretty sure that crocodiles don’t sob. The expression “to shed crocodile tears” has its roots in an ancient legend, according to which crocodiles pretend to weep to either lure or mourn their prey.

What I Remember From Med School

Reflex and emotional tears are produced by the lacrimal gland and drained through the nasolacrimal duct into the nose, which is why we also sniff when we cry. Any excess fluid spills out of the eyelid and trickles along the side of the nose or surface of the cheek, forming teardrops. Damage to the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve desensitizes the cornea, impairing the production of reflex tears. However, it is the parasympathetic division of the facial nerve that is responsible for making tears, and damage to the facial nerve, as in Bell’s palsy, can lead to a decrease in tear production.

Existential Tears

When we think of crying emotional tears, we think of sadness and grief. But we also shed emotional tears in response to a range of other, sometimes positive, emotions and feelings, including elation, laughter, love, frustration, pain, anger, and surprise. We may also cry in response to music, beauty, kindness, yearning, reunion, or anything that strikes us as poignant. What all these instances of crying have in common is not sadness, but significance.

Social Tears

Crying is not merely a private affair. Tears may serve a number of social functions. In particular, they may serve to convey our emotions while emphasizing their depth and sincerity; draw attention, sympathy, and assistance at a time of danger, distress, or need; and serve as a signal of appeasement, dependency, or attachment. If someone cries in our presence, it is almost impossible not to be moved, even changed, by that. No surprise, then, that tears can also be used to manipulate and deceive. The younger you are, the better you know this.

Healthy Tears

In ancient and medieval times, physicians believed that crying purged excess humors from the body. This idea survives in the modern scientific notion that emotional tears serve to excrete stress-related substances such as ACTH. But the more important purgation is, of course, psychological.

Crying may help us to feel better, in particular, by enabling us to experience, express, and “process” our emotions. In the Poetics, Aristotle argues that tragedy, by arousing emotions such as pity and fear, brings about a catharsis—a purgation or purification—of such emotions. After crying, we may feel not better exactly, but differently: calmer, clearer, more reconciled to life, or simply more certain of who we are and where we stand.

Crying as a Way of Knowing

Emotional tears signal moments that are of existential importance in our lives. They tell us that something matters deeply. Sometimes we know what that something is—the death of a parent, the birth of a child—but at other times our tears seem to know before we do, and to arrive bearing a message.

Imagine that a relationship or friendship has broken down. Three months later, or even three years later, you sit down on a park bench and unexpectedly begin to cry. Those tears tell you something that you may not have known, something that you may have been guarding against: that you still miss the relationship, and that it mattered more than you realized. The tragedy is when the other person also has their park bench moment, but neither of you acts upon it. Thirty years, gone like that.

We do not always cry because we know what matters to us. Sometimes we know what matters to us because we cry. In this sense, crying can be a way of knowing, revealing deeper truths that reason, thought, and language cannot reach. It sometimes happens that we cry without quite knowing why. When that happens, we should ask ourselves: What does this mean? What is the more refined part of me trying to tell me?

What brings us to tears changes as we change. A child might cry because they were underwhelmed by their Christmas presents. The sadness was real because, at that age, the presents really did matter. As we mature, the objects of our tears change along with our hierarchy of values. We cry less at the frustration of our immediate desires, and more at an unexpected kindness, a beautiful landscape, a piece of music, an abstract value like dignity or freedom, or the human condition.

We cry for our ex not merely because we can’t have them, but because they can’t have us.

How on earth will they cope?

item.title: What Looksmaxxing Reveals About Being Seen
item.description:
Body Image

What Looksmaxxing Reveals About Being Seen

When your face becomes evidence of the life you can expect.

Posted September 2, 2026

Source: Freepik / Freepik

A young man posts a photograph of his face online and asks strangers to rate him. The replies can be startlingly specific. His jaw is too narrow. His brow is weak. His eyes have the wrong tilt. Some people suggest a different haircut or better skin care. Others recommend fillers, hormones, or surgery.

In some looksmaxxing communities, he’s asking for more than an opinion about whether he’s attractive. His face is being treated as evidence of what kind of social life he can expect.

Looksmaxxing refers to efforts to maximize physical attractiveness, especially in online communities of boys and young men. The practices range from grooming, fitness, and skin care to cosmetic procedures and more extreme attempts to alter the face or body. In some communities, researchers have studied how looking better was described as a route to “ascension,” defined as a hoped-for movement upward in romantic and social status.

When a Face Predicts a Life

Sociologist Ozan Félix Sousbois studied 35 discussion threads from an incel- and lookism-oriented forum in which men posted photographs and sought ratings and surgical advice. Participants used appearance rankings to estimate where they stood in a romantic and social hierarchy. Improving their face was a way to gain attention, relationships, status, and belonging (Sousbois, 2025). In these communities, the score starts to function as a forecast of social life.

Appearance does affect how people respond to us, and research has shown this consistently. A major review of 11 meta-analyses found that people judged as attractive were generally evaluated and treated more positively than people judged as less attractive (Langlois and colleagues, 2000). But in looksmaxxing communities, that real social advantage can expand into a much larger explanation for loneliness, rejection, sexual success, respect, and personal worth.

Once appearance is treated as the cause of your social position, every feature acquires psychological weight. A disappointing date can become evidence about your jaw. Being ignored at a party can confirm a ranking. Rejection can feel like proof that your face has revealed where you belong.

Learning to See Yourself as a Ranking

Michael Halpin and colleagues analyzed 8,072 comments from a large looksmaxxing forum. Users scrutinized facial asymmetry, brow ridges, height, muscularity, and other features, often presenting their judgments as objective facts. Advice ranged from exercise to major body-altering procedures. The researchers also found that appearance judgments could become judgments about masculinity itself. A perceived physical shortcoming could be treated as evidence that a person was inadequate to be a man (Halpin and colleagues, 2025).

Social media research suggests that repeated comparison and evaluation can also change how people look at themselves. A 2025 meta-analysis of 83 studies involving more than 55,000 participants found that greater online social comparison was associated with greater body-image concerns and lower positive body image (Bonfanti and colleagues, 2025). Another 2025 meta-analysis found an association between social media use and self-objectification, the tendency to monitor yourself increasingly from an observer’s point of view (Wang and colleagues, 2025).

Looksmaxxing makes that observer’s position unusually explicit. You inspect your face as another person might inspect it, identify the defects, compare them with a standard, and decide what must be corrected. The question can shift from “How do I feel about how I look?” to “What does my appearance tell other people about my value?”

When Being Seen Becomes Being Ranked

In my forthcoming book, Being Seen, I explore the difference between being noticed, being evaluated, and being known. Looksmaxxing brings that distinction into sharp focus. If a favorable appearance is expected to produce attention, attraction, status, and belonging, then changing how you look can feel like a way of controlling how deeply other people will value you.

Someone may become more conventionally attractive and receive more favorable attention. But it can’t guarantee intimacy, respect, friendship, or accurate understanding. Yet if appearance is your explanation for why those things are missing, the logical response is to keep working on your appearance.

This is where optimization becomes psychologically important. Optimization has no obvious stopping point. Once you divide your face into measurable features, improvement in one area can direct attention toward another. Better skin doesn’t settle the question of the jaw. A stronger jaw doesn't settle the question of hair, height, body composition, or facial proportions. If the goal is to like how you look, then “good enough” is possible. If the goal is to maximize your position in a social hierarchy, then there’s always somewhere higher to climb.

The result is a peculiar form of visibility. You may become intensely preoccupied with how you are seen while experiencing yourself less as a whole person and more as a collection of features that other people are presumed to be judging.

Looksmaxxing reveals something larger than an extreme beauty trend. It shows what can happen when appearance becomes a theory of your social life. A face becomes an explanation for who notices you, who desires you, who respects you, and where you belong.

The most important question may be whether you have begun asking your appearance to determine what kind of life you are entitled to have. Once being seen becomes being ranked, changing the face can start to feel like changing the future. That’s why the promise is so powerful, and why it can become so difficult to know when the project is finished.

Copyright 2026 Tara Well, PhD

item.title: What Are Your Rules for Being Okay?
item.description:
Self-Esteem

What Are Your Rules for Being Okay?

The hidden conditions driving your self-worth.

Posted September 2, 2026

Key points
  • Consider the implicit requirements you carry to feel okay or good enough.
  • These rules often play out without a person's conscious awareness.
  • When rules are violated you may go into fix-it mode, which keeps you on a perpetual hamster wheel.
  • Developing conscious awareness for your rules brings you back into your real life, right now.

It’s natural to want things to go well in your life. You want your relationships to feel secure, your children to be happy, your work to be meaningful. You want to feel liked, interesting, included. It feels good to be in the sun, and we want to be in the sun as much as possible.

The problem is when these wants become rules or requirements for you to be okay.

I want my child to be happy becomes I can’t be okay if my child is struggling.

I want to feel included becomes if I am not included, something is wrong with me.

I want this relationship to work becomes if this relationship doesn’t work, I am unlovable.

I want my job to be successful becomes if my job is not successful, I am insignificant.

I want my body to look good becomes if my body doesn’t look good, I have less worth.

I want to be emotionally grounded becomes if I am upset or emotionally off, then I am unstable.

I want others to like me becomes if someone is upset with me, there is something wrong with me.

I want my life to look a certain way becomes if my life doesn’t look the way I thought it would, I failed.

These rules often play out without a person’s conscious awareness. You feel uneasy at the end of a meeting, a day, or a social event. Were your self-worth rules violated?

Many people in this situation ruminate and overthink their “error.” Then, they chase the next opportunity to redeem themselves. This can start to feel compulsive; you are constantly trying to get things right enough to feel okay. This can set up a hamster wheel of working harder and harder to feel okay, but never quite getting there.

Another sacrifice: You miss out on your actual life. Living by these rules requires your vigilance. You monitor your actions, how others react to you, and whether things are going the way you need them to go.

Letting go of at least some of that watchfulness is a risk. You may miss out on someone seeing you or be left out of something that matters. Someone may misread you; they perceive a weird vibe. Nonetheless, trying to prevent those experiences means you are managing your life like a scoreboard, constantly gauging whether you’re up or down.

The freedom to be who you are in a particular moment is worth the risk of getting something wrong.

How do these rules develop?

For most people, these rules for being okay develop early through learning what brought caregivers close to you, what made you feel loved and liked, and how you felt safe. If you learned that being easy and adaptable prevented conflict, then not being that way may mean you violated an important rule you have for staying safe in relationships. If being an achiever made you feel seen and important, then when you are not achieving, you may feel you are breaking that rule and suddenly feel insignificant and invisible. What begins as a strategy to keep people close eventually becomes a requirement for maintaining self-worth.

These rules may no longer be necessary or even relevant to your life now in adulthood, and yet you’re still living by them.

Develop awareness of your rules

The next time you find yourself triggered or upset by an event in your life, instead of trying to fix it immediately, ask yourself which of your rules might have been violated.

What did you subtly tell yourself needed to happen to be okay in this situation that didn’t happen?

Then ask yourself: What does it say about you when an expectation you needed to happen didn’t happen?

For example:

I needed to feel seen and valued for my accomplishment.

They didn’t notice, so I am unimportant.

I need my child to do well.

If my child struggles, I am failing as a parent.

I need people to be happy with me.

If someone is disappointed in me, I’m a disappointment.

Instead of keeping score of how well you’re doing in your life, start making a game out of catching yourself when you notice you’re keeping score. There can be something kind of funny about recognizing just how many rules you’ve been trying to follow! That awareness can break the spell and help you give up the scoreboard and return to the life happening around you.

Seek out the sunshine and enjoy those wonderful moments when everything in your world seems to align. Notice, however, when a desire is becoming a requirement. You can want to be accomplished, want your child to thrive, or want a relationship to work without making these things conditions of your worth. When something feels like it has to happen, or you are triggered because it didn’t happen, stop and ask yourself: What rule for being okay is making this feel so threatening right now?

item.title: When Thought Loses Its Address
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

When Thought Loses Its Address

How agentic AI takes thinking out of any single mind.

Posted September 2, 2026

Key points
  • Interacting AI agents form conviction and consensus with no center and no thinker.
  • Cognition loses its address as outcomes belong to the system, not any mind.
  • We may start the question and get the answer while absent from the thinking.
Source: Image by MJH Shikder from Pixabay.

Today, I can across a rather timely and interesting paper titled Physics of Agents: Statistical Mechanics Predicts Collective Behavior of AI Agents. It looked at what happens when AI agents begin interacting with one another like today’s agentic AI. In this study, the researchers created communities of large language model agents and allowed them to freely interact. Over time, the authors found that the LLM created "collective states that informed the decision-making process.

But there's more and worth a closer look. On mathematical problems with objectively correct answers, LLM interactions tended to improve "collective" accuracy. In other words, the correct agents exerted greater influence than incorrect ones. And this producing what the authors describe as an emergent truth-seeking tendency.

Now the “opinion” twist: On subjective political questions, conviction could still increase even without an objective truth toward which the group could converge. (Note to self: reread Animal Farm.)

The researchers found that these rather interesting behaviors could be described using ideas from good old-fashioned statistical mechanics that examined the interactions between particles. But in this study, the interactions weren't atoms in motion or magnetic spins. They were AI agents.

So, down another rabbit hole I went, and found myself interested in what this suggested about intelligence itself. When consequential behavior emerges through interactions among agents, where does that intelligence actually reside?

When Cognition Loses Its Address

Statistical mechanics, scary as it might sound, may help make this clearer. A single molecule doesn't have a temperature, but temperature appears when molecules move around in a container—the faster the hotter.

In this context, the idea of a "collective state" is particularly interesting to me. When it’s applied to AI agents, it begins to take on a life of its own. Consensus—like temperature— belongs to the collective in a way that can't be assigned to any one participant.

Of course, collective states aren't unique to AI. From politics to the marketplace, systems can develop behaviors that spring from those groups. But what makes agentic AI unusual (and fascinating) is that these artificial systems are collectively performing sophisticated intellectual tasks that may be greater than the sum of the parts.

We humans are accustomed to cognition having an address. We locate it somewhere, usually in a person. And even collective human intelligence the thinking subjects remain within the network. So far, so good.

Agentic AI can complicate this and give me reason to pause. With one LLM, we might still consider that model as the source of the answer. But with a network of agents, even locating the process that produced the answer becomes more difficult, if not impossible.

This reflects an idea I wrote about in March 2025 called the Cognitive DAO. I wondered if intelligence might emerge across a decentralized network without residing in any single mind. I described it then as intelligence that could be "expressed, not possessed" and perhaps more specifically, "coordinated, not centralized." Today, these new agentic systems give that question a bit more credibility and relevance. Here’s the key point: we may be approaching cognition without a defined center.

So, our persistent and pesky question about whether an individual AI can think may be becoming too narrow. Intelligence may increasingly be expressed through its individual architecture and its collective relationships. And maybe the better unit of analysis is beginning to expand from the individual model to the system in which it participates—a technological big bang.

The Human Enters the System

I think it’s fair to say that personal agents will increasingly act and, dare I say, "think" on our behalf. The pathway between a human question and its eventual answer may pass through a network of artificial agents. Importantly, we may not perceive or participate in this new found cognitive dynamic. And if more of the “work” occurs within these networks, our relationship to the cognition producing the answer shifts or even disconnected.

That raises another question around cognitive selfhood, or the sustained presence of the self in its own thinking. Agentic systems make that question more complicated because the boundaries of the cognitive process itself are expanding and becoming harder to define.

Today, AI is beginning to complicate many assumptions about thought and the thinker. If intelligence can increasingly emerge through interactions across a technological system, the question isn’t simply if AI can think. We may also need to ask where the thinking is happening, and what it means for us to remain present within it.
